explanation: A positive snapback test, in which the lower lid fails to return promptly against the globe after being pulled away without a blink, is the specific bedside sign of horizontal eyelid laxity from stretched canthal tendons and tarsus, and that laxity is the dominant mechanism allowing the lid margin and lashes to turn inward. Involutional entropion is multifactorial: horizontal laxity, attenuation or disinsertion of the lower lid retractors, and overriding of the preseptal orbicularis over the pretarsal portion. Option B fuses those last two mechanisms into a phrase that does not exist, since it is the orbicularis that overrides and the retractors that dehisce. A weak preseptal orbicularis (C) contributes to lid eversion problems rather than entropion, and levator dehiscence (D) causes aponeurotic ptosis of the upper lid, and neither is what the snapback test measures.

Deterioration after three days of oral antibiotics, with spread beyond the sac into adjacent tissues, means oral therapy has failed and the acute dacryocystitis has become a periorbital or preseptal cellulitis, so the patient should be admitted for intravenous antibiotics with imaging if orbital extension is suspected. Probing or irrigating the lacrimal system (C) is contraindicated in acute infection because it risks disseminating the infection and creating a false passage. DCR (D) is the definitive treatment for the underlying nasolacrimal duct obstruction but is deferred until the acute inflammation has settled. Incision and drainage (A) is not wrong in principle and is appropriate for a pointing, fluctuant lacrimal sac abscess, but it is an adjunct performed under systemic antibiotic cover rather than the single next step; in practice most patients are admitted, started on intravenous antibiotics, and drained during the same admission.

The ductules draining the orbital lobe pass through or alongside the palpebral lobe before opening into the superior fornix, so secretion from the entire gland funnels through the palpebral lobe region. That single anatomical fact is exactly why a biopsy should be taken from the orbital lobe rather than the palpebral lobe, making D false: cutting the palpebral lobe can transect the ductules of the whole gland and produce a dry eye. The lacrimal gland sits in the lacrimal gland fossa of the frontal bone (A is false), whereas the lacrimal sac fossa is formed by the lacrimal bone and maxilla. Eyelid eversion exposes the palpebral lobe, not the orbital lobe, so B is also false.

I cannot see the lesion, so this is answered on principle. Reconstruction of a full-thickness eyelid defect is chosen by defect size relative to total lid length: up to roughly a quarter to a third can usually be closed directly, and more in an elderly patient with lax lids; about a third to a half needs the closure relaxed with lateral cantholysis or a Tenzel semicircular flap; and beyond half a lid-sharing procedure such as a Hughes or Cutler-Beard flap with a graft is required. If the photograph shows a small, well-defined lid margin tumour, primary closure is the expected answer, and it is always the preferred option when the wound can be apposed without tension or lid margin notching.
concern: The answer depends on a lesion photograph I cannot see. If the tumour occupies more than about a third of the lid margin, the semicircular Tenzel flap becomes the correct choice.

explanation: A large salmon-pink conjunctival patch with a dense monotonous lymphoid infiltrate on histology is conjunctival lymphoma, usually of extranodal marginal zone (MALT) type. Once systemic imaging and haematological staging have excluded disseminated disease, localized low-dose external beam radiotherapy is the standard treatment for a large ocular adnexal lesion and achieves high rates of local control. Observation (A) is reserved for small indolent lesions or patients unfit for treatment; excision alone (D) is diagnostic rather than curative because the infiltrate is diffuse and margins cannot be cleared; and systemic chemotherapy or rituximab (C) is directed at disseminated disease. The examinable sequence is biopsy, then systemic staging, then local radiotherapy, because finding systemic disease switches management from local to systemic therapy.

A well-circumscribed, encapsulated, homogeneously enhancing intraconal mass causing slowly progressive axial proptosis with an acquired hyperopic shift, the latter from indentation and shortening of the posterior globe, is the classic profile of orbital cavernous haemangioma, now more properly called cavernous venous malformation. Enlargement during pregnancy is characteristic, since these lesions expand with hormonal change and increased blood volume. Lipodermoid (B) is a congenital epibulbar choristoma of the superotemporal fornix, not a retrobulbar enhancing mass. Lymphangioma (C) is irregular and non-encapsulated and usually presents in childhood with abrupt proptosis from haemorrhage into a chocolate cyst, and solitary fibrous tumour or haemangiopericytoma (D) is far rarer, grows faster and has less well-defined margins.

Thyroid eye disease is driven by autoantigens shared between the thyroid and the orbital fibroblast, principally the TSH receptor together with the IGF-1 receptor. Autoantibody engagement of those fibroblast receptors triggers glycosaminoglycan secretion, fibroblast proliferation, and differentiation into adipocytes or myofibroblasts, and the resulting hydrophilic matrix and fat expansion enlarge the extraocular muscles and orbital fat to produce proptosis and congestion. A cell-mediated component is genuinely present, since activated fibroblasts release T cell chemoattractants and the two populations amplify each other, so option A is not biologically false, merely not the initiating event the question is after. The clinical proof of the fibroblast receptor hypothesis is the efficacy of teprotumumab, an IGF-1 receptor blocking antibody.

Flat, light brown, perilimbal and interpalpebral conjunctival pigmentation in an elderly darkly pigmented patient is complexion-associated (racial) melanosis, which is benign, usually bilateral, moves freely over the sclera, and requires only observation with baseline photographs and periodic review. The features that would instead demand action are nodularity or thickening, feeder vessels, involvement of the palpebral conjunctiva, fornix or caruncle, or new pigmentation arising in a lightly pigmented adult, none of which is described. Metastatic work-up (A) and PSA (B) chase a systemic malignancy for which there is no evidence here. Wide excision with 4 mm margins (D) is the approach to conjunctival melanoma and would be substantial over-treatment; the slow darkening over years is a reason to document photographically and follow, not to excise.

Botulinum toxin chemodenervation is an established temporizing treatment for spastic entropion, where injection into the pretarsal and preseptal orbicularis stops the muscle riding up and inverting the lid margin while definitive surgery is planned. It does not treat ptosis (C); it causes ptosis when it diffuses to the levator. It has no accepted role in Marcus Gunn jaw winking (B), which is a misdirected trigeminal to levator synkinesis managed surgically. Lagophthalmos (D) deserves a caveat, because toxin is deliberately used to induce a protective ptosis in paralytic lagophthalmos with exposure keratopathy, so that option is defensible too; entropion remains the best single answer because it is the classical oculoplastic toxin indication.
concern: Option D is also a legitimate use of botulinum toxin (induced protective ptosis in paralytic lagophthalmos), so the item as recalled has two arguably correct answers.

explanation: A sudden fall in vision in a patient being treated for orbital cellulitis means an orbital or subperiosteal abscess, orbital compartment syndrome, or intracranial or cavernous sinus extension until proven otherwise, and urgent contrast-enhanced CT of the orbits, sinuses and brain is what identifies a collection needing surgical drainage and prompts a change in antibiotic cover. Asking about the duration of visual loss (A) does not alter the immediate plan. Measuring intraocular pressure (B) is by no means wasted and should happen at the bedside in the same minute, because tense proptosis with a markedly raised pressure and an afferent pupillary defect is orbital compartment syndrome requiring immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis before any scan. As a single best answer, urgent imaging is the step that changes management for the most likely underlying cause.

A soft, mobile, glistening yellow subconjunctival mass appearing in a 71-year-old and slowly prolapsing between the lids is orbital fat herniating anteriorly through an attenuated Tenon capsule, typically in the superotemporal quadrant and more common in older or heavier patients. Lipodermoid (A) is a congenital choristoma present from birth at the lateral canthal region, so it cannot appear de novo at 71. Solitary fibrous tumour or haemangiopericytoma (B) is a firm retrobulbar mass presenting with proptosis, and lacrimal gland pleomorphic adenoma (D) is a firm superotemporal orbital mass producing non-axial proptosis and lid fullness, not a soft yellow subconjunctival lesion. The management point is that prolapsed fat is benign and only needs excision for comfort or cosmesis.

Giant cell arteritis with established visual loss is the one presentation where pulsed intravenous methylprednisolone is preferred to starting with oral prednisone, because the fellow eye is at high risk over the following days and the aim is maximal immediate suppression; usual regimens are 0.5 to 1 g daily for three days followed by oral prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day. Oral prednisone 40 to 60 mg daily (A and B) is the correct starting therapy for giant cell arteritis without visual involvement, which is why B is the tempting answer here. Option D is internally impossible, since 40 mg/kg of prednisone is not a real dose and methotrexate is a weak steroid-sparing adjunct rather than an initial rescue drug. Treatment must never wait for the temporal artery biopsy, which stays positive for one to two weeks after steroids are begun, and in a diabetic patient the answer is to treat and cover the glycaemia, with tocilizumab considered early as the steroid-sparing agent.
concern: The source key of 60 mg oral prednisone is the standard regimen for giant cell arteritis without visual loss. This patient has established visual loss, and guideline practice is intravenous pulse methylprednisolone first, then oral prednisone. Diabetes is a reason to plan glycaemic cover and early steroid-sparing therapy, not to withhold pulse steroid. I flag this at moderate strength only because the recall may have intended a stem without established visual loss.

explanation: A migraineur with an episodically larger pupil that still reacts to light, full ocular motility, no ptosis and 20/20 acuity fits benign episodic unilateral mydriasis, a recognized migraine-associated phenomenon of transient autonomic imbalance, and the appropriate response is reassurance with outpatient review. A compressive third nerve palsy from a posterior communicating artery aneurysm can be set aside because it presents with ptosis and a motility deficit alongside a poorly reactive pupil, so urgent MRI and MRA (A) is not mandated by this examination. Admission (B) adds nothing when the examination is otherwise normal, and organophosphate toxicity (D) produces miosis, not mydriasis. It remains correct to ask about inadvertent contact with anticholinergic agents and to look for the light-near dissociation and sectoral palsy of a tonic pupil, and to review promptly if any new sign appears.

Vision in morning glory disc anomaly is unpredictable and spans nearly the whole range, from near-normal 20/20 down to light perception, depending on how much of the optic nerve and papillomacular bundle is involved, so the option stating the widest realistic range is correct. Most affected eyes in practice sit around 20/100 to 20/200 with an enlarged blind spot, but quoting a narrow band such as better than 20/80 (A) or hand motions to counting fingers (D) misrepresents the variability, and no light perception (B) is not the rule. The associations that matter clinically are serous retinal detachment in roughly a third of eyes, and basal encephalocele, midline central nervous system anomalies and moyamoya disease, so neuroimaging is indicated in these children.

Bilateral severe visual loss on waking from prolonged cardiac or spinal surgery, with poorly reactive pupils and a completely normal fundus, is perioperative posterior ischaemic optic neuropathy, in which the infarct is retrobulbar so the discs look normal for four to six weeks before pallor develops. Prolonged operative time, hypotension, anaemia, large fluid shifts and raised venous pressure are the recognized risk factors. Both anterior forms (B and C) are excluded by the normal fundus, since anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy requires disc oedema at presentation, and simultaneous bilateral arteritic disease in this setting would be exceptional. Dorsal midbrain syndrome (D) does produce light-near dissociation, but with upgaze palsy, convergence-retraction nystagmus and preserved acuity rather than hand motions vision.

On the reading given in the source note, the fields show a junctional pattern, that is a central or generalized defect in one eye with a superotemporal defect in the fellow eye, which localizes to the junction of the optic nerve and chiasm and is best captured among these options by a chiasmal lesion. A pure optic neuropathy (A) cannot account for any defect in the fellow eye. An optic tract lesion (B) produces a homonymous hemianopia respecting the vertical midline, characteristically incongruous, often with a contralateral relative afferent pupillary defect and band atrophy of the contralateral disc. An occipital lesion (D) gives a congruous homonymous defect, frequently with macular sparing.
concern: I cannot see the field printout and the source itself was undecided between chiasmal and optic tract. If both eyes show homonymous defects respecting the vertical midline, the answer is optic tract; if one eye shows a central defect and the fellow eye a superotemporal defect, it is a junctional scotoma and chiasmal is correct.

explanation: A unilateral dermatomal eruption of the forehead and periorbital skin evolving from erythema to papules to pustules and then crusting over two to three weeks, with pain preceding the rash, is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, reactivation of varicella zoster virus within the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve and its ganglion. The facial nerve (A) is motor to the face and is the nerve of Ramsay Hunt syndrome, in which vesicles appear in the ear canal and pinna with a facial palsy. The oculomotor (C) and trochlear (D) nerves supply extraocular muscles and would cause diplopia rather than a painful dermatomal rash. Vesicles on the tip or side of the nose (Hutchinson sign) indicate nasociliary branch involvement and predict intraocular disease, which is why every such patient needs a slit-lamp examination and pressure check.

The optokinetic drum is confirmatory because the optokinetic response is a reflex that cannot be voluntarily suppressed; if the eyes follow the rotating stripes, the visual pathway is intact to at least roughly 20/400, which is incompatible with claimed total blindness. Absence of a relative afferent pupillary defect (B) is only supportive, since symmetrical bilateral disease, chiasmal lesions and cortical blindness can all occur without an afferent defect. Failure of proprioceptive tasks such as touching the fingertips together (A) is suggestive, because proprioception does not require sight and a genuinely blind person performs it easily, but it is a soft sign rather than proof. Absence of eye movement on the mirror test (C) is what you would expect in genuine blindness, so it argues against rather than for non-organic loss.

Ocular motor apraxia is a failure to initiate voluntary horizontal saccades, which is why affected children develop the characteristic head thrusts: a blink and head turn drag the eyes onto the target, then the head rotates back while the vestibulo-ocular reflex holds fixation. Vertical saccades (B) are typically preserved in the congenital (Cogan) form, and that dissociation is the key bedside discriminator. Smooth pursuit (C and D) and the vestibulo-ocular reflex are intact, since the defect is specific to saccade initiation rather than to the ocular motor apparatus itself. Associated conditions worth excluding include ataxia-telangiectasia, Joubert syndrome and other cerebellar vermis and posterior fossa anomalies, so these children warrant neurological assessment.

Transposition has three steps: add the cylinder power algebraically to the sphere, reverse the sign of the cylinder, and change the axis by 90 degrees. Because this stem states that the cylinder sign has already been switched for you, the remaining arithmetic is expressed as subtracting the now-positive cylinder from the sphere and rotating the axis by 90 degrees. Worked example: +3.00 -1.00 x 90 becomes +2.00 +1.00 x 180, where the new sphere is +3.00 plus the original -1.00, which is identical to +3.00 minus the new +1.00. Options B and C fail immediately because the axis is always changed by 90 degrees and never by 180, which would simply return you to the same meridian.
concern: This is a wording-dependent item. The rule as normally memorized is to add the cylinder algebraically to the sphere, which is option A; D is correct only because the stem has already flipped the cylinder sign for the candidate. Both encode the same transposition, and the clearly wrong options are the two using 180 degrees.

explanation: The conventional order of subjective refraction using the Jackson cross cylinder is best sphere first, then refine the cylinder axis, then refine the cylinder power, then rebalance the sphere, so the third step is cylinder power. Axis precedes power because a misaligned axis makes the power endpoint unreliable, whereas an approximately correct power still permits the axis to be found accurately. The final sphere check is not optional: each 0.50 D change in cylinder power requires a 0.25 D change of sphere in the opposite direction to keep the circle of least confusion on the retina. Option C describes that closing step rather than the third one.

This child has high AC/A accommodative esotropia: the full cycloplegic correction straightens the eyes at distance but leaves 15 prism dioptres of esotropia at near, so the treatment is a bifocal, conventionally a +2.50 to +3.00 add in a flat-top or executive design with the segment set high, at or just crossing the lower pupillary margin, so that the child genuinely looks through it. Single-vision lenses leave the near deviation untreated, and a small, low-set segment at the usual adult height is the classic wrong panel because a child will simply look over it. I cannot see the four photographs, so I cannot confirm which panel is which; the correct one should show a wide flat-top or executive segment placed high on the lens.
concern: The answer depends on which lettered photograph shows a high-set executive or flat-top bifocal, and I cannot see the images.

explanation: Answered from definitions, since I cannot see the figure. The pupillary axis is the line perpendicular to the corneal surface passing through the centre of the entrance pupil; the visual axis runs from the fixation point through the nodal points to the fovea; and the optical axis is the best-fit line through the centres of curvature of the refracting surfaces. Angle kappa (C) is not a line at all but the angle between the pupillary axis and the visual axis, which is why it can generally be eliminated when a question asks what a drawn line represents. In the standard textbook diagram, the line reaching the fovea is the visual axis while the line drawn perpendicular to the cornea through the pupil centre is the pupillary axis, and the clinical relevance is that a large positive angle kappa mimics exotropia on Hirschberg testing.
concern: Entirely figure-dependent. If the red line runs from the fixation target to the fovea, the answer is the visual axis instead.

explanation: A pigmented conjunctival lesion in an 11-year-old is a nevus until proven otherwise; conjunctival melanoma is essentially a disease of middle-aged and older adults and is exceptionally rare in children, and primary acquired melanosis likewise arises in adults. The histological signature of a juvenile compound conjunctival nevus is nests of bland melanocytes at the epithelial-stromal junction and within the substantia propria, characteristically with intralesional epithelial inclusion cysts, and those cysts are a strongly reassuring feature. Melanoma (C) would show cytologically atypical cells with pagetoid intraepithelial spread, invasive nests and mitoses. Nevi commonly darken and enlarge around puberty and with inflammation, which is usually what prompts the referral, and the cysts can be seen at the slit lamp before any biopsy.

In a young adult with follicular conjunctivitis, the cytology that establishes adult inclusion conjunctivitis is a mixed lymphocytic and neutrophilic reaction with basophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies within epithelial cells on Giemsa staining. Gonococcal conjunctivitis (B) is hyperacute with copious purulent discharge, lid oedema and preauricular adenopathy, and its smear shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci inside neutrophils, a quite different picture, with the added danger of rapid corneal perforation. Because chlamydial conjunctivitis at this age is sexually transmitted, management is oral azithromycin or doxycycline plus treatment of sexual partners and screening for coinfection, not topical therapy alone. I cannot see the slide, so the identification rests on the clinical framing and the answer options offered.

If the histology shows nests and sheets of atypical squamous cells with keratin pearls, intercellular bridges and dyskeratosis, then squamous cell carcinoma is correct. The discriminators to look for on the slide are basaloid lobules with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact from the surrounding stroma for basal cell carcinoma, foamy lipid-laden vacuolated cytoplasm with pagetoid intraepithelial spread and positive lipid staining for sebaceous carcinoma, and a benign acanthotic proliferation with horn cysts and no atypia for seborrhoeic keratosis. Clinically the two features that should raise suspicion for sebaceous carcinoma in any lid lesion are loss of lashes and a recurrent unilateral blepharoconjunctivitis, since it is the great masquerader of the eyelid.
concern: I cannot see the slide, and the clinical prior strongly favours basal cell carcinoma, which accounts for the large majority of ulcerated lower lid malignancies. The source answer is correct only if the histology demonstrates keratinizing squamous differentiation. Treat this item as image-dependent.

explanation: Moxifloxacin is a fourth-generation fluoroquinolone that inhibits bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking the supercoiling and separation of replicating DNA, so it interrupts DNA replication and is bactericidal. Inhibition of cell wall synthesis (A) describes the beta-lactams, vancomycin and bacitracin. Inhibition of protein synthesis (C) describes aminoglycosides, macrolides, tetracyclines and chloramphenicol. Disruption of membrane permeability (D) is the mechanism of polymyxin B. The dual target of later-generation quinolones is what broadens gram-positive cover and raises the barrier to resistance compared with ciprofloxacin, and moxifloxacin is preservative-free with good intraocular penetration, which is why it is widely used perioperatively.

Sarcoidosis in a young African American patient with hilar lymphadenopathy produces granulomatous uveitis, and the classic photographic finding is large greasy mutton-fat keratic precipitates on the inferior corneal endothelium in Arlt triangle. Those deposits are aggregates of macrophages together with the epithelioid cells and multinucleated giant cells that macrophages become on activation, which is why options A and C describe essentially the same cell lineage rather than genuinely competing answers. Lymphocytes and neutrophils (B and D) constitute the small fine keratic precipitates of non-granulomatous uveitis such as HLA-B27 associated disease. I cannot see the photograph, but the same granulomatous logic applies if it shows a Koeppe or Busacca iris nodule instead.
concern: Image-dependent, and the item is internally weak because epithelioid cells are activated macrophages, so options A and C are not cleanly separable.

explanation: Aqueous humor is not a simple ultrafiltrate of plasma but an actively secreted fluid, and its composition reflects that active secretion. Relative to plasma it carries a marked excess of ascorbate (roughly 15 to 20 times), lactate and pyruvate, and a deficit of protein, and it is slightly more acidic with a small excess of hydrogen and chloride ions, so options A, B and D all move in the wrong direction. Bicarbonate is the component present in relative deficit in human aqueous. This is more than trivia: carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary epithelium generates the bicarbonate that drives sodium transport and therefore aqueous formation, which is exactly why carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce secretion and lower intraocular pressure.

Chronic cicatrizing conjunctivitis with fornix foreshortening and symblepharon, combined with linear deposition of immunoglobulin and complement along the conjunctival epithelial basement membrane zone on direct immunofluorescence, is ocular mucous membrane pemphigoid, historically ocular cicatricial pemphigoid, a type II hypersensitivity against basement membrane antigens. Stevens-Johnson syndrome (B) also scars the conjunctiva but follows an acute drug or infection-triggered episode with skin and mucosal sloughing rather than a slowly progressive course, and it does not show linear basement membrane immunoreactants. The clinical message is that this disease needs systemic immunomodulation, dapsone for milder disease and rituximab or intravenous immunoglobulin for aggressive disease, because topical treatment alone does not halt progression. The biopsy should be taken from uninvolved or minimally involved bulbar conjunctiva, since surgery on inflamed tissue can itself accelerate scarring.

An oil droplet appearance on retroillumination is anterior lenticonus, and anterior lenticonus with sensorineural hearing loss is Alport syndrome, an inherited disorder of type IV collagen whose central problem is a progressive haematuric nephropathy, so nephrology is the correct referral. The same collagen defect makes the anterior lens capsule abnormally thin, which explains reports of spontaneous capsule rupture and the need for care during cataract surgery. Other ocular clues to seek are the dot-and-fleck retinopathy of the perimacular and midperipheral retina and, less often, posterior polymorphous-like corneal changes. Endocrine (B) and cardiology (C) referral do not follow from lenticonus with deafness; note also that a true oil droplet reflex in an infant without deafness should raise galactosaemia instead.

The accepted safety threshold for conventional epithelium-off corneal cross-linking is 400 microns of stromal thickness after epithelial removal and before ultraviolet A exposure, because below that depth the endothelium receives an irradiance above its damage threshold and endothelial decompensation may follow. Thinner corneas are managed with modified protocols such as hypo-osmolar riboflavin to swell the stroma, contact lens-assisted cross-linking, or transepithelial techniques, rather than simply proceeding. Two practical points: the 400 micron figure refers to the de-epithelialized stroma and not to preoperative pachymetry, and thickness should be rechecked after riboflavin loading because the cornea dehydrates and thins during the soak.

An endothelial keratoplasty lenticule is thinner centrally than peripherally, a negative meniscus, which steepens the posterior corneal curvature relative to the anterior surface and reduces total corneal power, producing a hyperopic shift typically around +0.75 to +1.25 dioptres after DSEK. That is precisely why the surgeon aims for a myopic target of about -0.75 to -1.25 when performing cataract surgery in an eye that will need or has had DSEK; this patient sitting at -0.25 will end up hyperopic. A myopic shift (D) is the opposite of what the lenticule geometry produces. Induced regular astigmatism (B) is small because the graft is inserted through a small incision rather than sutured circumferentially, and DMEK causes a much smaller hyperopic shift because that graft is essentially uniform in thickness.

Woody, fibrin-rich pseudomembranes that recur on the tarsal conjunctiva are ligneous conjunctivitis, caused by type 1 plasminogen deficiency: without plasminogen the fibrin laid down during mucosal inflammation cannot be cleared by fibrinolysis and accumulates as the characteristic wood-like membrane. The same defect affects other mucosae, so ask about gingival, respiratory, middle ear and genitourinary involvement, and be aware of occlusive hydrocephalus in severe cases. Treatment aims to replace the missing activity, with topical plasminogen where available, fresh frozen plasma, and adjuncts such as topical heparin, steroid or ciclosporin; excision alone is followed by prompt recurrence. Transferrin deficiency (B) is not a described mechanism, and collagenase overexpression (C) drives corneal melting in other conditions rather than membrane formation.

The principle being tested is where the globe is weakest and where an occult rupture hides. The sclera is thinnest just behind the insertions of the rectus muscles and at the limbus, so blunt rupture classically occurs anteriorly, running parallel and concentric to the limbus, often superonasally, and it may occur at a site remote from or opposite the point of impact by a contrecoup mechanism. The signs to hunt for are an abnormally deep or shallow anterior chamber, dense bullous subconjunctival haemorrhage with chemosis, low intraocular pressure, a peaked or irregular pupil, and vitreous haemorrhage. Where rupture is suspected the examination continues in theatre, with exploration extending beneath the rectus insertions, and all pressure on the globe must be avoided until then.
concern: This is a poorly written recall. The rectus muscle insertions (B) and the superonasal perilimbal quadrant (C) are equally classical rupture sites and the source itself was undecided. I have followed the source key because the contrecoup, limbus-parallel anterior rupture is the most commonly taught pattern, but no single option is uniquely correct as worded.

explanation: Stromal oedema with keratic precipitates and anterior chamber cells in an eye with a previous dendritic keratitis but an intact epithelium is herpetic stromal keratitis with endotheliitis, an immune-mediated process, so the treatment is a topical corticosteroid to suppress inflammation together with a systemic antiviral to prevent epithelial reactivation while the eye is on steroid. Oral aciclovir or valaciclovir is preferred over a topical antiviral (B) because topical agents such as trifluridine and ganciclovir are epitheliotoxic with prolonged use and penetrate the stroma poorly. Systemic steroid (C and D) is unnecessary for isolated corneal inflammation and adds avoidable systemic risk. The essential safety check before starting steroid is the absence of epithelial ulceration or a dendrite, which the stem confirms with no fluorescein uptake, and the steroid is then tapered very slowly, sometimes over months, with antiviral cover maintained throughout.

Irritation that is worst on waking, in an obese patient who is difficult to position at the slit lamp, with diffuse punctate epithelial staining, is floppy eyelid syndrome: the tarsus is rubbery and lax, the upper lid everts spontaneously against the pillow overnight, and the exposed papillary tarsal conjunctiva and cornea are chronically abraded. The diagnostic manoeuvre is effortless eversion of the upper lid with gentle superior traction, and the papillary reaction is on the upper tarsus. Thygeson superficial punctate keratitis (B) is a bilateral, recurrent, central coarse epithelial keratitis with a white quiet conjunctiva, unrelated to body habitus or time of day. The systemic point that matters most is the strong association with obstructive sleep apnoea, which should be asked about and referred, alongside night-time lubrication, taping or shielding, and horizontal lid tightening if conservative measures fail.

On the Roper-Hall classification, grade II is corneal haze through which iris details remain visible, with less than one third of the limbus ischaemic, which is exactly what is described. Grade I is epithelial damage only with no limbal ischaemia; grade III is total epithelial loss with stromal haze obscuring iris details and one third to one half limbal ischaemia; grade IV is an opaque cornea with more than half the limbus ischaemic and carries the worst prognosis. Limbal ischaemia is the prognostic driver because it reflects loss of limbal stem cells, which is also why the newer Dua classification grades by clock hours of limbal involvement and percentage of conjunctival involvement. Whatever the grade, immediate copious irrigation until the pH normalizes precedes any attempt at classification.

Conjunctivalization of the cornea with keratinization after a severe alkali burn is total limbal stem cell deficiency, and no corneal graft can survive on a surface with no source of corneal epithelium, so the stem cell population must be restored first, by autologous limbal or cultivated limbal epithelial transplantation if the fellow eye is healthy, or by allograft with systemic immunosuppression if the injury is bilateral. Lamellar or penetrating keratoplasty (A and B) placed on a stem-cell-deficient bed will simply be recovered by conjunctival epithelium and fail. A keratoprosthesis (C) is a legitimate option but is reserved for eyes that have failed keratoplasty or have bilateral end-stage keratinized disease, and it carries lifelong risks of glaucoma, endophthalmitis and melt. Lids, tear film and inflammation must be optimized before any of these procedures.

Superotemporal lens subluxation with stretched but intact zonules points to Marfan syndrome, and the systemic association that matters, because it can kill the patient, is aortic root dilatation with the risk of dissection, so echocardiography and cardiology referral are mandatory. The internal logic of the item also helps: homocystinuria, the main alternative, dislocates the lens inferonasally and would make both intellectual disability (B) and thromboembolism (D) correct simultaneously, which cannot be the intended single answer. The referral for poor school performance is most simply explained by uncorrected lenticular myopia and astigmatism rather than by cognitive impairment. Marfan patients are typically tall with arachnodactyly rather than short (C), and the practical ocular point is that these eyes need dilated peripheral retinal examination because of the high lifetime risk of retinal detachment.

Schirmer I is performed without topical anaesthetic, so the strip itself irritates the ocular surface and the result reflects basal plus reflex secretion; less than 10 mm of wetting in 5 minutes is abnormal and less than 5 mm is severe. The basic secretion test is the identical procedure done after instilling anaesthetic, which largely removes the reflex component. Schirmer II (D) adds deliberate nasal mucosal stimulation specifically to isolate reflex secretion, so it is a reflex test rather than a combined one. Tear break-up time (B) measures tear film stability rather than production, and the dye disappearance test (C) assesses lacrimal outflow, so neither addresses the question asked.

In a patient with sickle cell disease or trait, intraocular pressure is the measurement that changes management, because red cells sickle in the hypoxic acidotic environment of the anterior chamber, obstruct the trabecular meshwork and produce pressure spikes, and the sickle optic nerve and retinal circulation tolerate raised pressure very poorly, so the threshold for surgical evacuation is much lower than usual. Management is altered as well: carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are avoided because systemic acidosis and haemoconcentration promote further sickling, and hyperosmotics are used cautiously for the same reason. Visual acuity (A) and ultrasonography (C) belong to a complete assessment but carry nothing like the same decision weight, and B-scan is reserved for a view-obscuring hyphema when posterior segment injury is suspected. Every patient of African, Mediterranean, Middle Eastern or Indian ancestry with traumatic hyphema should have sickle status checked.

Two separate factors rule this patient out of LASIK. First, the tissue required to correct around ten dioptres of myopia threatens the residual stromal bed even in a thick cornea once flap thickness is subtracted, and thin residual beds are the classical route to iatrogenic ectasia. Second, the starting keratometry of 40 dioptres is flat, so ablating that much would leave a postoperative central K in the low thirties, well below the accepted floor of roughly 34 to 35 dioptres, with predictable loss of optical quality, night vision symptoms and regression. The discrepancy between manifest and cycloplegic refraction also signals accommodative over-minusing, so treating the manifest figure (A) would overcorrect, but choosing any single number (B or C) does not address the underlying anatomical unsuitability. The appropriate discussion is a phakic intraocular lens such as an ICL, or refractive lens exchange in an older patient.

Redness and photophobia appearing a few days after blunt ocular trauma, with an intact epithelium and no fluorescein uptake, is traumatic iridocyclitis; expect cells and flare in the anterior chamber, a smaller sluggish pupil, and a pressure that may be low or raised. Recurrent corneal erosion (B) would produce sharp pain on waking with a definite epithelial defect or loose epithelium that stains, which the stem explicitly excludes. Treatment is a topical steroid tapered over one to two weeks with a cycloplegic for comfort and to prevent posterior synechiae. Because this followed blunt trauma, the examination must also include gonioscopy for angle recession and a dilated peripheral retinal examination, with long-term pressure monitoring.

Peripheral corneal stromal thinning progressing from ten to fifty per cent in a patient with rheumatoid arthritis is peripheral ulcerative keratitis, and the governing principle is that this is an ocular manifestation of systemic vasculitis rather than a local surface problem. Untreated it carries substantial mortality from extra-articular vasculitic disease, so the treatment that changes the outcome is systemic immunosuppression, with methotrexate a reasonable steroid-sparing agent and cyclophosphamide or rituximab for aggressive or perforating disease, alongside systemic steroid for immediate control. Increased lubrication (D) has already failed and is only supportive. Conjunctival resection or recession (A) is a recognized adjunct that removes a local source of collagenases and immune cells, and is most associated with Mooren ulcer, but it does not touch the systemic driver, and a tectonic graft (C) is reserved for impending or actual perforation and will melt again if the underlying inflammation is unsuppressed.
concern: I disagree with the source key. In rheumatoid peripheral ulcerative keratitis the intervention that alters both the ocular and the systemic outcome is systemic immunosuppression; local surgical measures such as conjunctival resection are adjunctive only. Topical steroid alone can accelerate stromal melt, which is a further reason the systemic steroid-sparing agent is the answer here.

explanation: The false statement is the timing of rebleeding: secondary haemorrhage after traumatic hyphema characteristically occurs in the first two to five days as the clot retracts and lyses, and the risk is largely past by about a week rather than beginning at three weeks. The other three statements are true: red cells and inflammatory debris obstruct the trabecular meshwork so the pressure rises, hyphema typically follows blunt trauma tearing the iris root or the ciliary body face, and rest with head elevation, a protective shield and avoidance of antiplatelet drugs is standard care. Rebleeding matters because it is associated with higher pressures, corneal blood staining and worse visual outcomes, and it is more frequent in patients of African descent and in sickle cell disease.

When corneal scrapes and cultures are negative in a keratitis that is not improving, particularly after trauma involving organic matter, the next step is corneal biopsy, which samples deeper stroma where fungi, Acanthamoeba, mycobacteria and Nocardia can lie beyond the reach of a superficial scrape; the specimen should be divided between histopathology and microbiology on appropriate media. Confocal microscopy is a valuable non-invasive adjunct where available but does not replace tissue when the diagnosis is still unknown. Starting steroids (C) before an organism is identified risks accelerating a fungal or amoebic infection. A viral culture (B) does not fit a post-traumatic suppurative keratitis. Pausing antimicrobials for a day or two before the biopsy improves the yield.

In a rhegmatogenous detachment the single factor dictating how quickly you must operate is whether the fovea is still attached, because visual prognosis falls sharply once the macula detaches; a macula-on detachment is therefore treated as urgent, ideally within about 24 hours, and especially so when the detachment is superior and bullous and advancing towards the fovea. Duration (B) governs urgency mainly in macula-off eyes, where the discussion concerns how much benefit remains in operating within the first week, and it is less relevant while the macula is still on. Age (C) and break size (D) influence the choice of technique and the risk of proliferative vitreoretinopathy rather than the timing. Positioning the patient to limit further spread while awaiting theatre is a useful practical measure.

The earliest objective sign of hydroxychloroquine retinopathy is parafoveal disruption and thinning of the outer retinal layers on spectral domain OCT, seen as loss of the ellipsoid zone and thinning of the outer nuclear layer in a perifoveal ring, well before anything is visible at the fundus. Screening pairs SD-OCT with automated 10-2 visual fields, using 24-2 or 30-2 fields in Asian patients in whom damage is often pericentral and extramacular, with fundus autofluorescence and multifocal ERG as adjuncts. RPE mottling and bull's eye maculopathy (C) are late and largely irreversible. A central scotoma on Amsler testing (B) is insensitive and subjective, and bone spicules (D) belong to retinitis pigmentosa and thioridazine toxicity. The dosing principle to carry away is that risk rises with cumulative dose and with a daily dose above 5 mg/kg of real body weight, and with renal impairment or concurrent tamoxifen.

Acute central retinal artery occlusion causes ischaemic oedema of the inner retina, appearing on OCT as thickening with increased reflectivity of the nerve fibre, ganglion cell and inner plexiform layers extending into the inner half of the inner nuclear layer, precisely because that territory is supplied by the retinal circulation while the outer retina is nourished by the choroid. The hyperreflective inner band also shadows the layers beneath it, and over following weeks it gives way to inner retinal atrophy and thinning. Central retinal vein occlusion (A) produces intraretinal and cystoid oedema with haemorrhages rather than this uniform inner retinal band. Central serous chorioretinopathy (C) shows subretinal fluid with a thickened choroid, and glaucoma (D) causes chronic ganglion cell and nerve fibre layer thinning without acute hyperreflectivity.

Standardized A-scan echography best characterizes a choroidal melanoma, because the tumour shows a high initial spike from its anterior surface followed by low to medium internal reflectivity with a regularly decreasing pattern, often with spontaneous internal vascular pulsations; B-scan adds the dome or collar-stud shape, choroidal excavation and acoustic hollowing, and ultrasound also provides the thickness and basal dimensions that determine treatment. UBM (A) images only the anterior 4 to 5 mm and is the tool for iris and ciliary body lesions rather than a posterior choroidal mass. OCT (C) beautifully demonstrates overlying subretinal fluid and RPE change but cannot penetrate a thick tumour to assess internal structure or height. The discriminating value of reflectivity is shown by choroidal haemangioma, which is high in internal reflectivity, the opposite of melanoma.

Axial length greater than 25 mm, that is a long myopic eye, is the strongest risk factor for retinal detachment following Nd:YAG capsulotomy, since such eyes already have liquefied vitreous, lattice degeneration and a high baseline detachment risk, and disrupting the posterior capsule permits forward vitreous movement and traction. The other recognized risks are younger age and male sex, so old age (B) and female sex (C) are the reverse of the truth. Lens material (D) influences the rate of capsular opacification but is not a meaningful detachment risk factor. Practical mitigation is to defer capsulotomy where vision permits, use the smallest effective opening at the lowest energy, and examine the peripheral retina before and after the procedure.

Needle marks identify intravenous drug use, and the organism to fear in that context is Bacillus cereus, which causes a fulminant endophthalmitis evolving over hours with severe pain, proptosis, a ring corneal infiltrate and fever, and which frequently destroys the eye despite treatment; intravitreal vancomycin with early vitrectomy is the response. Klebsiella (B) is the classic organism of endogenous endophthalmitis complicating a pyogenic liver abscess, particularly in diabetic patients in East Asia, and it too produces choroidal or subretinal abscess but in that systemic setting. In real practice the commonest endogenous ocular infection in an injecting drug user with a focal chorioretinal lesion is Candida, and the source note confirms it was deliberately omitted from the choices, so Bacillus is the intended answer. Endogenous endophthalmitis always requires blood cultures and a hunt for the systemic source, including echocardiography for endocarditis.

The treatment threshold for macular oedema in branch retinal vein occlusion derives from the Branch Vein Occlusion Study: persistent macular oedema involving the fovea with vision of 20/40 or worse, after allowing roughly three months for spontaneous improvement. Modern first-line therapy is intravitreal anti-VEGF injection, with grid laser or a steroid implant as alternatives, but the entry criterion is unchanged. Macular thickening or exudate within 500 microns of the fovea (B and C) are criteria for clinically significant macular oedema in diabetic retinopathy, a different disease and a different trial. The extent of non-perfusion (D) predicts neovascularization and therefore guides scatter laser, not treatment of the oedema itself.

Applying the 4-2-1 rule, severe non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy is diagnosed when any one of the following is present: intraretinal haemorrhages and microaneurysms in all four quadrants, venous beading in two or more quadrants, or intraretinal microvascular abnormalities in at least one quadrant. Haemorrhages and microaneurysms in all four quadrants therefore meets the criterion for severe NPDR. Cotton wool spots are markers of ischaemia but do not enter the 4-2-1 count and neither upgrade nor downgrade the grading. Proliferative disease (D) requires new vessels or a vitreous or preretinal haemorrhage, which is not described. The clinical importance is the high one-year rate of progression from severe NPDR to proliferative disease, which justifies close follow-up and consideration of earlier intervention.

Ischaemic hypertensive retinopathy is signalled by the same signs of capillary closure that indicate ischaemia anywhere in the retina, and among these pairs venous beading with retinal neovascularization is the combination in which both elements require significant capillary non-perfusion. Hard exudates (D) reflect leakage across an incompetent blood-retina barrier rather than ischaemia, and microaneurysms (A) are non-specific and appear early with any vascular dysfunction. Blot haemorrhages with IRMA (C) is the tempting distractor because IRMA genuinely indicates ischaemia, but blot haemorrhages alone merely reflect deep intraretinal bleeding, so the pair is less specific than B. In a hypertensive patient, retinal new vessels should also prompt a search for coexisting vein occlusion, diabetes or ocular ischaemic syndrome.

For zone I retinopathy of prematurity with plus disease, the randomized evidence favours intravitreal bevacizumab over conventional laser, showing a markedly lower recurrence rate in zone I stage 3 plus disease while preserving peripheral retina and giving better refractive outcomes than ablating it. Laser (B) remains the treatment of choice for zone II disease and is still the definitive option wherever reliable follow-up cannot be guaranteed. Cryotherapy (A) is historical and has been superseded by laser. Intravitreal steroid (D) has no established role in ROP. Two caveats belong with the anti-VEGF answer: recurrence occurs late, often around 45 to 55 weeks postmenstrual age, so prolonged and reliable follow-up is mandatory, and retinal vascularization remains incomplete for months afterwards.

In the Endophthalmitis Vitrectomy Study the intervention was determined by presenting acuity: eyes with light perception only benefited from immediate pars plana vitrectomy, whereas eyes seeing hand motions or better did equally well with a vitreous tap and injection of intravitreal antibiotics, conventionally vancomycin plus ceftazidime, with a sample sent for Gram stain and culture. This patient sees hand motions, so tap and inject is correct and the absence of a vitrectomy option is not a problem. Topical antibiotics (B) do not reach therapeutic vitreous levels and are adjunctive only. Steroids (C) have a role as an adjunct once antibiotic cover is established but never as primary treatment. Many surgeons now intervene with vitrectomy earlier than the trial protocol given improved instrumentation, but the tap-and-inject threshold remains the examinable answer.

An eye with sudden severe pain, a pressure of 60 and a cloudy cornea is presumed acute angle closure, and the first move is medical pressure reduction, beginning with topical agents (a beta blocker, an alpha-2 agonist, and pilocarpine once the pressure has fallen enough for the ischaemic iris sphincter to respond) together with a systemic carbonic anhydrase inhibitor. Definitive laser peripheral iridotomy (D) treats the underlying pupil block but can rarely be performed through an oedematous cornea, so it follows medical clearing, and surgical iridectomy (A) is reserved for when laser is impossible. Hyperosmotic agents (C) are not wrong and are commonly added when the pressure is very high or refractory in order to clear the cornea enough for laser, which is presumably why the source hesitated, but they carry cardiovascular, renal and diabetic risks and are second-line rather than the initial step. Compression gonioscopy and supine positioning help, and the fellow eye needs a prophylactic iridotomy.

Argon laser peripheral iridoplasty deliberately uses low-energy, long-duration, large-spot burns to contract the peripheral iris stroma and pull the iris away from the trabecular meshwork: a 500 micron spot, a duration of about 0.5 seconds, and power of roughly 200 to 300 milliwatts, titrated to visible iris contraction without bubble formation or an audible pop. The 800 milliwatt setting is far too hot and risks iris burn-through, marked inflammation, pigment dispersion, corneal endothelial damage and peripheral anterior synechiae. Note that the printed duration of 0.5 msec in this recall must be a transcription error, since the defining feature of iridoplasty is its long exposure, the opposite of the short high-energy pulses used for iridotomy. Iridoplasty is most useful in plateau iris configuration and in acute angle closure that does not break with medical therapy.
